title: Interrogative, Indefinite and Relative Pronouns
description: τίς and τις, indirect and deliberative questions, the relative pronoun ὅς, and conditional relative clauses with ἄν or ἐάν and the subjunctive.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html:
τίς, τί, who? which? what?, is a third-declension word with the masculine and feminine alike. Its acute accent never turns grave: τί λέγει; what does he say? The neuter τί often means why?: τί ποιεῖτε ταῦτα; why do you do these things? The indefinite τις, τι, someone, something, a certain one, has the same forms but is enclitic: ἄνθρωπός τις, a certain man; εἶπέν τις, someone said. Both can stand with a noun or alone.

An indirect question keeps the mood and tense of the direct question behind it, as indirect discourse does: ἠρώτησεν αὐτὸν τίς ἐστιν, he asked him who he was (he asked, Who are you?). A deliberative question, which expects an answer in the imperative, has the subjunctive: τί ποιήσωμεν; what shall we do?

The relative pronoun ὅς, ἥ, ὅ, who, which, is declined like an ordinary adjective of the second and first declension, with ὅ in the neuter singular. It agrees with its antecedent in gender and number but takes its case from its own clause: ὁ ἀπόστολος ὃν εἶδες, the apostle whom you saw. A relative that would be accusative is often attracted into the genitive or dative of its antecedent (ἐπὶ πᾶσιν οἷς ἐποίει, at all the things which he was doing). The antecedent is often left out: ὃς … he who; ἃ … the things which, what.

English relatives in -ever (whoever, whatever, wherever, whenever) are expressed by the relative with ἄν or ἐάν and the subjunctive: ὃς ἂν πιστεύσῃ σωθήσεται, whoever believes will be saved; ὅταν (ὅτε ἄν) ἔλθῃ, whenever he comes.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: τίς (who?) has an acute that never becomes grave; τις (someone) is enclitic and usually has no accent of its own. ἥ, οἵ, αἵ (relative) are accented; ἡ, οἱ, αἱ (article) are not. ὅ (which) is not ὁ (the), and ὅτι (that, because) is not ὅ τι. In λέγω ὃ ἔχω, what is the thing which (relative ὅ); in λέγω τί ἔχω, what is a question (interrogative τί). ποῦ; (where?) asks; ὅπου (where) relates. εἰ in an indirect question means whether.

blocks.caption: Source
blocks.html: Machen, *New Testament Greek for Beginners* (1923), Lesson 27 (p. 170). Words Machen does not list but the New Testament uses 50 times or more are added with glosses after Jeffrey Dodson's Greek-English lexicon (public domain).
